title: |
  Does Partisan Attachment Amplify Affective Polarization?
subtitle: |
  Vertical and Horizontal Dimensions Across 25 European Democracies
abstract: |
  Affective polarization (AP) research faces a persistent measurement challenge: should partisans be identified through self-reported attachment or vote choice? This distinction matters theoretically -- identity accounts predict attachment amplifies polarization, while categorization accounts suggest vote anchors suffice -- and comparatively, as explicit attachment rates vary widely across European democracies. We introduce *partisan type* (explicit versus implicit partisans) and test whether subjective attachment differentially predicts *vertical* AP (party-targeted attitudes) versus *horizontal* AP (citizen-targeted behavior). Analyzing thermometer ratings and conjoint trust-game data from 25 countries (N≈29,800), we find explicit partisans exhibit significantly higher vertical AP than implicit partisans, but the two groups show no difference in horizontal behavioral discrimination. These results reveal distinct psychological mechanisms: subjective attachment shapes party affect but not interpersonal behavior. For comparative research, our findings validate combining vote-anchored and attachment-based samples for behavioral studies while cautioning that restricting to explicit identifiers may misrepresent attitudinal polarization's behavioral translation in multiparty systems.

## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Affective polarization (AP)—the tendency to favor one's own partisan group while disliking opponents—has emerged as a defining feature of contemporary democracies [@iyengar2012affect; @iyengar2019origins; @boxell2024cross].
Beyond policy disagreement, AP encompasses social distancing, interpersonal hostility, and discriminatory behavior toward partisan outgroups, raising concerns about democratic cooperation and political stability [@graham2020democracy; @kingzette2021affective; @berntzen2023consequencesofaffective].
Extensive research now documents AP's prevalence across advanced democracies [@wagner2021affective; @reiljan2020fear; @reiljan2024patterns], yet fundamental questions persist about its measurement and psychological foundations.
A particularly consequential ambiguity concerns who counts as "partisan" in empirical analyses: should researchers restrict samples to citizens who self-report feeling attached to a party, or include all those who reveal partisan preferences through vote choice regardless of reported attachment?
This operationalization choice carries major implications for both theory and comparative inference, yet existing research has not systematically examined whether these two groups exhibit equivalent levels of affective polarization.

The partisan identification question matters theoretically because it implicates competing accounts of AP's underlying mechanisms.
Social identity perspectives emphasize subjective attachment as a psychological bond that intensifies emotional investment in political groups, predicting that explicit partisan identifiers should exhibit stronger polarization than those who merely vote without reporting felt attachment [@huddy2015expressive; @mason2018one; @iyengar2015fear].
In contrast, categorization and cue-processing accounts suggest that partisan labels and vote anchors provide sufficient information to generate polarized responses even absent subjective identification [@orr2023affective; @orr2020policy; @dafoe2018information].
Distinguishing these mechanisms has proven difficult because party cues simultaneously signal group membership and ideological content, producing observational equivalence [@orr2023affective].
The partisan type distinction—explicit versus implicit partisanship—provides analytical leverage: systematic differences between these groups would support identity-centric accounts, while equivalent behavior would challenge the assumption that subjective attachment drives polarization.

The measurement stakes are especially high in comparative multiparty research.
Unlike the U.S. two-party system, European electorates contain substantial proportions of voters who express stable partisan preferences yet deny feeling attached to any party.
The prevalence of explicit partisan attachment varies dramatically—ranging from roughly 40% to 80% across European countries in our data—meaning that restricting analyses to self-identified partisans reshapes the population of inference differently in each national context and undermines cross-national comparability [@rollicke2023polarisation; @TorcalComellas2025Operationalizing].
Moreover, widely used AP measures diverge precisely in their treatment of partisans: @reiljan2020fear's Affective Polarization Index (API) focuses on reported identifiers, while @wagner2021affective's spread measure encompasses all voters, yielding potentially different empirical portraits of polarization [@campos2025new; @CarlinLove2025Measuring].
Without systematic evidence on whether explicit and implicit partisans exhibit equivalent AP, researchers face arbitrary decisions about sample inclusion that may distort substantive conclusions and comparative inference.

Recent theoretical refinements further complicate these issues by distinguishing *vertical* AP—attitudes toward parties and elites—from *horizontal* AP—behavior toward fellow citizens [@klar2018affective; @areal2024verticalvshorizontal; @druckman2019we].
This differentiation matters because different manifestations of polarization may arise from different psychological mechanisms and carry distinct normative implications [@Berntzen2025PoliticalViolence; @campos2025new].
If subjective partisan attachment shapes how citizens feel about *parties* but not how they treat partisan *others* in interpersonal contexts, then vertical and horizontal AP would require separate theoretical accounts.
Testing whether partisan type differentially predicts these two dimensions could reveal whether attachment-driven and categorization-driven processes operate in parallel, with the former dominating party-targeted attitudes and the latter governing citizen-targeted behavior—a possibility existing research has not explored.

We address these challenges by distinguishing *explicit* partisans—respondents who report feeling attached to a party—from *implicit* partisans—those who deny such attachment yet reveal partisan anchors through vote choice.
We term this distinction *partisan type*.
This conceptualization extends classic insights on independents, leaners, and implicit partisan identity [@petrocik2009measuring; @kinder2017neither; @theodoridis2017me; @elliott2024like] to multiparty systems, isolating a theoretical quantity prior work has not directly examined: whether self-reported attachment enhances polarization beyond the effects of partisan categorization alone.
Empirically, we analyze thermometer ratings (vertical AP) and conjoint trust-game experiments (horizontal AP) from 25 European democracies (N≈29,800), applying Bayesian hierarchical models with country-level random effects to estimate AP conditional on partisan type while accounting for respondent clustering and cross-national heterogeneity.

Our core findings reveal a striking asymmetry.
For vertical AP measured through party thermometer ratings, explicit partisans exhibit systematically and substantially higher polarization than implicit partisans across all 25 countries.
Yet for horizontal AP measured through token allocations in dictator and trust games embedding randomized partisan cues, explicit and implicit partisans discriminate identically: both groups show equivalent levels of AP.
This vertical-horizontal divergence challenges theories positing unified mechanisms underlying affective polarization.
Subjective attachment shapes *attitudes toward parties* but does not amplify *behavioral discrimination among citizens*.

Extending these findings, we examine individual-level moderators to identify what drives vertical AP and whether the explicit-implicit gap varies systematically with respondent characteristics.
Models incorporating interactions between partisan type and theoretically relevant covariates—ideological extremity, political interest, social identity strength—reveal that the attachment gap in vertical AP is larger among ideologically extreme and politically engaged respondents, consistent with identity consolidation mechanisms.
Yet these same moderators do not condition horizontal AP, where explicit and implicit partisans behave identically regardless of individual characteristics.
These patterns suggest attitudinal polarization toward parties reflects identity-driven processes amplified by attachment strength, while behavioral discrimination emerges from categorization and inferred alignment activated equally by vote anchors alone.

These results carry three major implications for affective polarization research.
First, for measurement and population definition, our findings validate combining vote-anchored and attachment-based respondents when estimating behavioral AP—there is no empirical reason to exclude implicit partisans from horizontal analyses, and doing so risks unnecessary loss of external validity.
Conversely, vertical AP studies restricting samples to explicit identifiers may overestimate attitudinal polarization's translation into discriminatory behavior, as attachment predicts party affect but not interpersonal conduct.
Second, for theories of partisan identity, the standard attachment item appears weakly related to behavioral discrimination.
Horizontal AP in Europe arises from categorization and inferred alignment rather than self-reported identity strength, challenging accounts that emphasize subjective attachment as AP's primary driver and highlighting the need for multidimensional frameworks distinguishing party-targeted and citizen-targeted polarization [@campos2025new; @IyengarWagner2025Conceptualizing].
Third, the cross-national consistency of our vertical-horizontal asymmetry across 25 diverse party systems suggests these patterns may represent structural features of multiparty polarization rather than country-specific idiosyncrasies, with potentially important implications for understanding how partisan conflict shapes democratic politics in fragmented electoral contexts.

The paper proceeds as follows.
Section 2 reviews theoretical perspectives on partisan identity and affective polarization, develops our conceptualization of partisan type, and derives testable hypotheses distinguishing vertical from horizontal AP.
Section 3 describes our data from 25 European democracies, measurement strategy applying @reiljan2020fear's API logic consistently across both dimensions, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling approach.
Section 4 presents main results showing the vertical-horizontal asymmetry in partisan type effects across pooled and country-specific analyses.
Section 5 examines individual-level drivers and moderators of vertical and horizontal AP.
Section 6 discusses theoretical and methodological implications for comparative polarization research and concludes.

## Theory {#sec-theory}

### Origin and Expansion of Affective Polarization Research {#sec-origins}

The contemporary study of political polarization was reshaped by the insight that partisan conflict is driven not only by ideological disagreement but also by social and emotional divisions [@iyengar2012affect].
Early work demonstrated that hostility between partisans intensified even while policy preferences remained comparatively stable [@fiorina2006culture; @fiorina2008polarization], redirecting scholarly attention from ideological distance [@poole1984polarization; @mccarty2006polarized] toward affective orientations between political groups.
Building on social identity approaches, affective polarization (AP) is typically defined as the tendency of individuals to feel warmth toward perceived ingroup members and hostility toward outgroups [@iyengar2015fear; @iyengar2019origins; @IyengarWagner2025Conceptualizing].

Rooted in Social Identity Theory and Self-Categorization Theory [@tajfel1979integrative; @tajfel1978differentiation; @turner1987rediscovering], AP reflects a broader and well-documented human propensity for ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation observable even in minimal group settings [@tajfel1971social; @sherif1961intergroup; @brewer1999psychology].
Political science research focuses on cases where the salient social identity is partisanship [@huddy2001political; @huddy2015expressive; @mason2015disrespectfully].
Over the past decade, this perspective has generated a large comparative literature documenting the prevalence of AP across advanced democracies [@wagner2021affective; @reiljan2020fear; @reiljan2024patterns; @boxell2024cross], identifying its drivers [@hobolt2024polarizing; @bail2018exposure; @orr2020policy; @mason2015disrespectfully; @tornberg2022digital; @luttig2017authoritarianism], tracing its consequences for democratic attitudes and behavior [@diermeier2019partisan; @berntzen2023consequencesofaffective; @kingzette2021affective; @graham2020democracy; @mcconnell2018economic; @broockman2023doesaffective], examining temporal trends [@iyengar2018strengthening], and evaluating interventions designed to reduce partisan hostility [@adams2023can; @kalla2022voter; @druckman2023does; @mernyk2022correcting].

The rapid growth of this research program has produced substantial empirical knowledge but also conceptual and measurement disputes [@campos2025new; @bakker2024putting; @IyengarWagner2025Conceptualizing; @CarlinLove2025Measuring].
Scholars increasingly recognize that the concept encompasses multiple related phenomena and that different operationalizations can yield divergent conclusions about its magnitude, distribution, and implications.
Consequently, cumulative knowledge now depends less on documenting whether AP exists than on clarifying what precisely is being measured and for whom theoretical claims apply.

### Core Debates and Conceptual Refinements {#sec-core-debates}

Early debates centered on whether polarization should be understood as a state or a process and whether its democratic consequences are uniformly harmful or conditional [@kingzette2021affective; @moore2020exaggerated; @westwood2022current].
More recent work emphasizes that different manifestations of AP may have distinct normative implications and psychological origins [@Berntzen2025PoliticalViolence; @broockman2023doesaffective; @voelkel2023interventions].
Three major refinements structure the contemporary literature.

First, target differentiation.
Scholars distinguish vertical polarization—affect toward parties and elites—from horizontal polarization—affect and behavior toward fellow citizens [@klar2018affective; @harteveld2021ticking; @druckman2019we; @areal2024verticalvshorizontal].
Vertical AP can further target parties or leaders [@reiljan2024patterns; @torcal2022affective], while horizontal AP concerns interpersonal discrimination.
Because elite-directed hostility and citizen-directed behavior may arise from different mechanisms, conflating them risks obscuring causal relationships.

Second, manifestation differentiation.
Research differentiates attitudinal AP, typically measured with feeling thermometers or social distance scales, from behavioral AP, measured through economic allocation decisions or real interactions [@druckman2019we; @CarlinLove2025Measuring; @iyengar2015fear].
These measures need not align: citizens may express dislike without discriminating behaviorally, or discriminate without reporting strong hostility.

Third, operationalization choices. Measurement depends on defining partisan groups.
Scholars must determine how to identify partisans (attachment vs vote choice), whether individuals may hold multiple ingroups [@kekkonen2021affective; @kekkonen2022puzzles; @bantel2023camps], how to define outgroups (least-liked party vs average opponent) [@wagner2021affective], and whether to include non-partisans in analysis [@rollicke2023polarisation].
These decisions reshape empirical findings rather than merely refining them.

Together, these developments imply that affective polarization is not a single phenomenon but a family of related outcomes whose interpretation depends heavily on conceptual and measurement choices [@campos2025new; @IyengarWagner2025Conceptualizing].

### Extending Affective Polarization to Multiparty Systems {#sec-extending-AP}

These challenges intensify in multiparty democracies [@rollicke2023polarisation; @TorcalComellas2025Operationalizing]. In two-party systems, ingroup and outgroup boundaries are clear.
In fragmented party systems, however, several ambiguities emerge.

First, it is unclear what constitutes the ingroup.
Researchers variously define it as the most-liked party, multiple parties, or ideological blocs [@kekkonen2021affective; @kekkonen2022puzzles; @bantel2023camps; @reiljan2021ideological]. Second, identifying membership can rely on subjective attachment or vote choice [@wagner2021affective; @reiljan2020fear].
Third, defining outgroups may involve the least-liked party or the average evaluation of all opponents [@wagner2021affective].
Finally, many citizens lack explicit partisan identification, raising the question of whether they belong in the population of inference [@garzia2023affective].

Existing measurement strategies address these issues differently.
Some approaches assign each respondent a single ingroup and calculate polarization relative to all outparties [@reiljan2020fear; @hahm2024divided]; others measure dispersion in party evaluations and include non-identifiers [@wagner2021affective]; still others allow multiple ingroups [@kekkonen2021affective; @kekkonen2022puzzles].
Because explicit partisan attachment varies substantially across European countries, these decisions affect cross-national comparability. Restricting analyses to self-identified partisans can approximate the electorate in countries with high identification rates but represent only a minority in others.
As a result, identical operationalizations may imply different target populations across cases.

Moreover, attachment questions themselves may capture different psychological phenomena depending on party system institutionalization and stability [@garzia2023affective].
Comparative research typically assumes equivalence, yet this assumption is rarely evaluated.

### Partisan Type, Population of Inference, and Research Contribution {#sec-contribution}

To address these comparability and interpretation problems, we distinguish between respondents who report attachment to a party and those who deny attachment but reveal a partisan anchor through vote choice. We refer to these categories as partisan types: explicit and implicit partisans. The distinction serves primarily as a consistent terminology allowing comparable analysis across contexts rather than a novel theoretical construct.

The distinction matters because it directly affects the population of inference. If the proportion of explicit and implicit identifiers varies across countries, analyses limited to explicit identifiers describe fundamentally different electorates across cases. Consequently, comparative conclusions about affective polarization may depend as much on sampling decisions as on political behavior.

Beyond measurement, the comparison offers leverage for adjudicating competing theoretical accounts of polarization. Social identity theories emphasize subjective attachment as a psychological bond that intensifies emotional investment in political groups [@huddy2015expressive; @mason2018one; @huddy2013group; @west2022partisanship]. In contrast, categorization and cue-processing perspectives suggest that partisan labels and vote anchors alone provide sufficient information to generate polarized responses, even absent felt attachment [@orr2023affective; @orr2020policy; @dafoe2018information; @tajfel1971social].

We therefore compare explicit and implicit partisans across two dimensions of affective polarization:
(1) vertical attitudinal polarization toward parties and
(2) horizontal behavioral discrimination toward citizens.
We further examine whether individual characteristics moderate these relationships. The analysis of individual-level drivers remains exploratory; covariate selection will be guided by existing research on ideological extremity [@abramowitz2006exploring; @abramowitz2008ispolarization], engagement [@luttig2017authoritarianism], social identity strength [@mason2015disrespectfully; @mason2018one], perceived threat [@huddy2015expressive], democratic norms [@graham2020democracy], social trust, and media consumption [@bail2018exposure; @tornberg2022digital].

### Hypotheses {#sec-hypotheses}

We evaluate competing explanations of AP by comparing explicit and implicit partisans across vertical (attitudinal) and horizontal (behavioral) domains. 
Social identity accounts emphasize subjective attachment as a psychological bond that intensifies affective investment in political groups [@huddy2015expressive; @mason2018one], whereas categorization accounts argue that partisan labels and vote anchors alone suffice to generate polarized responses [@orr2023affective; @dafoe2018information].

#### Vertical (Attitudinal) AP

If attachment creates emotional investment in political objects, explicit identifiers should evaluate ingroup and outgroup parties more differently than implicit identifiers.

$\text{H}_{1a}$ (Identity mechanism): Explicit partisans exhibit higher vertical affective polarization than implicit partisans.

If partisan categorization alone activates evaluative schemas, attachment adds little beyond knowing one's partisan anchor [@orr2023affective].

$\text{H}_{1b}$ (Categorization mechanism):
Explicit and implicit partisans exhibit equivalent vertical affective polarization.

#### Horizontal (Behavioral) AP

If identity strength drives discriminatory behavior toward political opponents, explicit identifiers should favor copartisans more strongly in interpersonal decisions [@huddy2015expressive; @iyengar2015fear].

$\text{H}_{2a}$ (Identity mechanism):
Explicit partisans exhibit higher horizontal affective polarization than implicit partisans.

If categorization and inferred alignment are sufficient to generate intergroup bias [@tajfel1971social; @sherif1961intergroup], behavioral discrimination should not depend on subjective attachment.

$\text{H}_{2b}$ (Categorization mechanism):
Explicit and implicit partisans exhibit equivalent horizontal affective polarization.

#### Individual-Level Moderation

Identity-based mechanisms imply that affective investment intensifies among individuals whose political orientations are psychologically consolidated [@mason2015disrespectfully; @west2022partisanship].

$\text{H}_3$: The explicit–implicit gap in vertical polarization is larger among ideologically extreme and politically engaged respondents.

If behavioral discrimination primarily follows categorization rather than identity strength, these moderators should not alter behavioral differences.

$\text{H}_4$: Individual-level moderators affect vertical but not horizontal differences between partisan types.

### The Rise of Affective Polarization Research

@iyengar2012affect's seminal work transformed polarization research by shifting focus from ideological disagreement toward affective and social dimensions of partisan conflict.
Their core insight—that partisan antipathy had intensified even as policy preferences remained relatively stable—catalyzed a vast research program investigating how citizens increasingly favor their own partisan group while disliking opponents.
This reconceptualization moved beyond traditional concerns about policy polarization [@poole1984polarization; @mccarty2006polarized] to emphasize social identity processes generating ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation.

Rooted in Social Identity Theory (SIT) and Self-Categorization Theory (SCT) [@tajfel1979integrative; @tajfel1978differentiation; @turner1987rediscovering], affective polarization (AP) captures the tendency of individuals to exhibit warmer feelings toward perceived ingroup members while expressing hostility toward outgroups.
Although fundamentally a universal human phenomenon observable across minimal group contexts [@tajfel1971social; @sherif1961intergroup], AP research in political science focuses specifically on politically salient identities, with partisanship serving as the primary axis of division.

The field has expanded rapidly, documenting AP's prevalence across advanced democracies [@wagner2021affective; @reiljan2020fear; @reiljan2024patterns; @boxell2024cross], investigating its drivers [@hobolt2024polarizing; @bail2018exposure; @orr2020policy; @mason2015disrespectfully; @tornberg2022digital], consequences [@diermeier2019partisan; @berntzen2023consequencesofaffective; @kingzette2021affective; @graham2020democracy], temporal dynamics [@iyengar2018strengthening], and potential interventions [@adams2023can; @kalla2022voter; @druckman2023does].
Yet this rapid expansion has generated conceptual ambiguities and measurement debates that complicate cumulative knowledge-building [@campos2025new; @bakker2024putting; @IyengarWagner2025Conceptualizing].

### Conceptual Refinements and Persistent Debates

Early AP research faced definitional ambiguities regarding whether polarization constitutes a *state* (current levels) versus a *process* (temporal trends), and whether its democratic implications are uniformly negative or contextually dependent [@kingzette2021affective; @moore2020exaggerated; @westwood2022current].
Recent work questions simplistic associations between AP and democratic erosion [@broockman2023doesaffective; @voelkel2023interventions], highlighting that different manifestations carry distinct normative implications.

Scholars have refined AP conceptualization along three key dimensions.
First, **target differentiation** distinguishes *vertical* or political AP—attitudes toward parties and political elites—from *horizontal* or social AP—behavior and affect toward fellow citizens [@klar2018affective; @harteveld2021ticking; @druckman2019we].
Vertical AP further subdivides into party-targeted (PAP) versus leader-targeted (LAP) affect [@reiljan2024patterns; @torcal2022affective].
This distinction matters because elite-directed and citizen-directed polarization may arise from different mechanisms and carry different consequences for democratic functioning [@Berntzen2025PoliticalViolence; @areal2024verticalvshorizontal].

Second, **manifestation differentiation** separates *attitudinal* or expressive AP—typically measured via feeling thermometers or social distance scales—from *behavioral* AP—observed through economic games, hiring decisions, or actual interactions [@druckman2019we; @CarlinLove2025Measuring].
Attitudinal and behavioral measures need not align: citizens may report partisan antipathy without translating it into discriminatory conduct, or vice versa.

Third, **operationalization choices** about partisan classification directly shape measurement.
Researchers must decide: How to define partisan ingroups—single most-liked party versus multiple affiliations or ideological blocs? [@kekkonen2021affective; @kekkonen2022puzzles; @bantel2023camps]
How to *identify* partisans—self-reported attachment versus vote choice? [@wagner2021affective; @reiljan2020fear]
How to define outgroups—least-liked party versus average across all opponents? [@wagner2021affective]
Whether to include or exclude non-partisans in the population of inference? [@rollicke2023polarisation]

These choices are not merely technical but reshape substantive conclusions about AP's magnitude, distribution, and correlates [@campos2025new; @TorcalComellas2025Operationalizing].

### Measurement Challenges in Multiparty Systems

Extending AP research to European multiparty systems intensifies these conceptual and measurement complications [@rollicke2023polarisation; @TorcalComellas2025Operationalizing].
Unlike the U.S. two-party context where ingroup-outgroup boundaries are straightforward, fragmented party systems create ambiguity about which parties constitute relevant comparison groups.

Three dominant thermometer-based approaches have emerged.
@reiljan2020fear's **Affective Polarization Index (API)** assigns each respondent a single ingroup (their most-liked or identified party) and calculates polarization as the difference between ingroup affect and the average affect toward all outparties.
@wagner2021affective's **spread measure** captures the overall dispersion (standard deviation) of party evaluations, accommodating voters who lack clear partisan anchors.
@wagner2021affective's **distance measure** calculates each respondent's mean affective distance from their most-liked party across all evaluations.

These measures diverge in critical ways.
Reiljan's API requires identifying partisans—traditionally through self-reported attachment—meaning it focuses on a subset of the electorate.
Wagner's spread encompasses all voters, including those without party identification.
Alternative approaches allow multiple ingroups or ideological blocs [@kekkonen2021affective; @kekkonen2022puzzles; @bantel2023camps; @reiljan2021ideological], attempting to capture multiparty identification dynamics more realistically.

Crucially, **the prevalence of explicit partisan attachment varies dramatically across European countries**—ranging from roughly 40% in some nations to over 80% in others (see Figure 1).
This cross-national heterogeneity creates a fundamental inferential problem: restricting analyses to self-identified partisans reshapes the population of inference differently in each country, undermining comparability.
A study sampling only explicit identifiers in Denmark (where they comprise ~80% of voters) draws conclusions about a near-universal population; the same approach in Latvia (where identifiers are ~40%) infers about a subset less than half the total sample.
External validity thus depends heavily on whether measurement choices match theoretical populations of interest—a consideration existing research rarely addresses systematically.

Moreover, the **partisan identification question itself** may function differently across contexts.
In established party systems with strong identification traditions, attachment items capture stable psychological bonds.
In newer democracies or volatile party systems, the same question may elicit different psychological phenomena—or substantial non-response [@garzia2023affective].
Yet comparative AP research typically treats the attachment item as functionally equivalent, potentially conflating distinct forms of partisan connection.

### Introducing Partisan Type: Explicit Versus Implicit Partisans

We address these conceptual and comparative challenges by introducing a generalizable distinction: **partisan type**.
We define *explicit partisans* as respondents who report feeling attached to a party, and *implicit partisans* as those who explicitly deny such attachment yet reveal partisan anchors through vote choice (retrospective or prospective).

This conceptualization extends classical insights on independents and "leaners" in American politics [@petrocik2009measuring; @kinder2017neither; @elliott2024like] to multiparty contexts.
Research on U.S. independent leaners demonstrates that voters who initially disclaim partisan identity but subsequently reveal party preference when probed often behave similarly to declared identifiers [@keith1992myth].
Work on implicit partisan identity [@theodoridis2017me; @hawkins2012motivated] shows that partisan cues activate identity-consistent behaviors even among those denying attachment.

We adopt the more general term *partisan type* rather than "leaner" because the latter presumes a two-pole structure where self-identified independents occupy a meaningful middle category—a metaphor that does not travel cleanly to fragmented multiparty systems where voters confront multiple ideological camps rather than a single left-right axis.
Nevertheless, the underlying theoretical logic is parallel: some voters affirm subjective attachment while others deny it, yet both groups possess behavioral partisan anchors.

The **theoretical utility of partisan type** lies in adjudicating between identity-based and categorization-based mechanisms underlying AP.
Social identity accounts predict that subjective attachment -- the feeling of belonging to a partisan group -- should amplify both affective responses and discriminatory behavior [@huddy2015expressive; @mason2018one].
If explicit attachment represents genuine identity strength, explicit partisans should exhibit stronger AP than implicit partisans across both attitudinal and behavioral domains.

Conversely, categorization and cue-processing accounts suggest that partisan labels trigger ideological inferences, normative expectations, and social categorization processes sufficient to generate polarization absent felt attachment [@orr2023affective; @dafoe2018information].
Under this view, vote choice provides enough informational content to activate discriminatory responses -- explicit atachement adds little beyond what categorization accomplishes.

To our knowledge, no existing comparative research systematically examines whether explicit and implicit partisans differ in their levels of affective polarization, despite this question's centrality to understanding AP's psychological foundations.

### Vertical Versus Horizontal Affective Polarization

Recent theoretical refinements distinguish vertical (elite-targeted) from horizontal (citizen-targeted) polarization [@harteveld2021ticking; @klar2018affective; @druckman2019we; @areal2024verticalvshorizontal].
This differentiation matters because different AP manifestations may arise from distinct psychological mechanisms and carry different normative implications.

**Vertical AP** captures attitudes toward parties, leaders, and political elites, typically measured via feeling thermometers.
If subjective partisan attachment amplifies emotional investment in political objects representing the ingroup, explicit partisans should exhibit systematically higher vertical AP than implicit partisans.
Identity theories emphasize that attachment creates psychological stakes in party success and symbolic representation [@mason2018one; @huddy2015expressive; @west2022partisanship], suggesting party-targeted affect should correlate with identity strength.

**Horizontal AP** captures behavioral discrimination among citizens, measured through allocation decisions, social distance, or interaction patterns.
If categorization and inferred alignment primarily drive interpersonal behavior, implicit partisans—despite denying attachment—should discriminate equivalently to explicit identifiers.
Minimal-group research demonstrates that shallow categorization alone generates intergroup bias [@tajfel1971social; @sherif1961intergroup], suggesting vote anchors may suffice to trigger behavioral discrimination without requiring subjective identity.

The vertical-horizontal distinction thus provides analytical leverage: if partisan type predicts vertical but not horizontal AP, this would imply dissociated mechanisms—attachment shaping party attitudes while categorization governing citizen behavior.
Such asymmetry would challenge unified identity theories and suggest the need for multidimensional frameworks [@campos2025new; @IyengarWagner2025Conceptualizing].

### Hypotheses

We formalize competing predictions regarding how partisan type should influence AP across vertical and horizontal dimensions.

#### Vertical (Attitudinal) Polarization

If subjective partisan attachment amplifies emotional responses to political objects:

**H1**: Explicit partisans exhibit *higher vertical AP* (party thermometer polarization) than implicit partisans.

This hypothesis follows directly from social identity logic: attachment should heighten affective investment in ingroup parties and antipathy toward outgroup parties.

#### Horizontal (Behavioral) Polarization

Two competing predictions emerge:

**H2a** (Identity mechanism): Explicit partisans exhibit *higher horizontal AP* (behavioral discrimination) than implicit partisans.

Under identity-centric accounts, attachment should amplify all forms of polarization, including citizen-targeted behavior.

**H2b** (Categorization mechanism): Explicit and implicit partisans exhibit *equivalent horizontal AP*.

Under categorization accounts, partisan cues and vote anchors suffice to generate behavioral discrimination absent felt attachment.

Our design allows testing whether horizontal AP follows vertical AP (supporting H2a and unified identity mechanisms) or diverges (supporting H2b and dissociated mechanisms).

#### Individual-Level Moderators

We further hypothesize that individual characteristics may amplify or dampen partisan type's influence:

**H3**: The explicit-implicit gap in vertical AP is *larger* among ideologically extreme and politically engaged respondents (identity consolidation).

**H4**: Individual-level moderators of vertical AP do *not* moderate horizontal AP differences between types (distinct mechanisms).

These hypotheses allow identifying not only whether partisan type matters, but *for whom* it matters most.

### Study Contributions

Our research contributes to affective polarization scholarship in four ways.

First, **conceptually**, we introduce partisan type as a generalizable framework for clarifying populations of inference in comparative research, extending U.S.-based insights on independents and implicit identity to multiparty systems.

Second, **empirically**, we document substantial cross-national variation in explicit-implicit distributions (Figure 1), demonstrating that measurement choices reshape generalizability differently across European democracies.

Third, **substantively**, we test whether subjective attachment amplifies polarization by comparing explicit and implicit partisans across two AP dimensions and 25 countries, providing the first systematic assessment of identity versus categorization mechanisms in comparative context.

Fourth, **for individual-level drivers**, we identify covariates predicting vertical and horizontal AP and test whether the same factors moderate partisan type effects, revealing whether attitudinal and behavioral polarization share common roots or emerge from distinct processes.

*Note: The individual-level driver analyses (H3/H4) remain to be conducted. We will survey existing literature on AP correlates -- e.g. ideological extremity, political interest, social identity strength, perceived threat, democratic norms, social trust, and media consumption -- to guide covariate selection.*

## Research design

### Data

The data are structured hierarchically with multiple nested levels:

- Level 4: Country ($c$)
- Level 3: Party anchor ($p$) - nested within country
- Level 2: Respondent ($i$) - nested within party-country
- Level 1: Observation (round/rating) ($r$) - nested within respondent

$$r \subset i \subset p \subset c$$

### Empirical Strategy

We employ a Bayesian hierarchical modeling approach. We apply the same model structure across studies, varying the outcome and predictor specifications to address distinct research questions. This unified framework enables systematic comparison of affective polarization across attitudinal and behavioral domains.

#### Base Model Structure

Both thermometer and token allocation models share the following hierarchical specification:

**Likelihood:**
$$
Y_{ripc} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{ripc}, \sigma^2)
$$

**Linear predictor:**
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{ripc} = &\alpha_0 + \alpha_c + \alpha_{p[c]} + \alpha_{i[pc]} \\
&+ \beta_1 \cdot \text{CoParty}_{r} \\
&+ \beta_2 \cdot \text{Explicit}_{i} \\
&+ \beta_3 \cdot (\text{CoParty}_{r} \times \text{Explicit}_{i}) \\
&+ \beta_{1c} \cdot \text{CoParty}_{r} \\
&+ \beta_{1p[c]} \cdot \text{CoParty}_{r} \\
&+ \beta_{3c} \cdot (\text{CoParty}_{r} \times \text{Explicit}_{i}) \\
&+ \boldsymbol{X}_{ripc}'\boldsymbol{\beta}
\end{aligned}
$$

where:

- $Y_{ripc}$ is the outcome (thermometer rating or token allocation)
- $\text{CoParty}_r$ is an indicator for whether the rated party (Study 1) or game partner (Studies 2-3) matches respondent $i$'s party anchor
- $\text{Explicit}_i$ indicates whether respondent $i$ reported explicit party attachment (vs. implicit partisanship via vote choice only)
- $\boldsymbol{X}_{ripc}$ includes controls (party size, ideological distance, etc.)

**Random effects:**
$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_c &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\text{country}}^2) && \text{Country intercepts} \\
\alpha_{p[c]} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\text{party}}^2) && \text{Party intercepts (within country)} \\
\alpha_{i[pc]} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\text{respondent}}^2) && \text{Respondent intercepts (within party)} \\
\beta_{1c} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\text{AP,country}}^2) && \text{Country-varying AP effect} \\
\beta_{1p[c]} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\text{AP,party}}^2) && \text{Party-varying AP effect} \\
\beta_{3c} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\text{interaction,country}}^2) && \text{Country-varying type effect}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Priors:**
$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_0 &\sim \mathcal{N}(50, 20^2) && \text{Grand intercept} \\
\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3, \boldsymbol{\beta} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 10^2) && \text{Fixed effects} \\
\sigma_{\text{country}}, \sigma_{\text{party}}, \sigma_{\text{respondent}} &\sim \text{Exp}(1) && \text{Random effect SDs} \\
\sigma_{\text{AP,country}}, \sigma_{\text{AP,party}}, \sigma_{\text{interaction,country}} &\sim \text{Exp}(1) && \text{Random slope SDs} \\
\sigma &\sim \text{Exp}(1) && \text{Residual SD}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Study 1: Operationalizing Attitudinal Affective Polarization

**Research Question:** How do alternative operationalizations of partisanship and thermometer-based indices affect estimates of attitudinal AP?

**Outcome:** $Y_{ripc} = \text{Rating}_{ripc}$ (thermometer score, 0-100 scale)

**Model:**
$$
\text{Rating}_{ripc} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{ripc}, \sigma^2)
$$

with $\mu_{ripc}$ specified as in the base model above.

**Key parameters:**

- $\beta_1$: Average affective polarization effect (co-party premium in ratings)
- $\beta_3$: Differential AP between explicit and implicit partisans
- $\beta_{1c}$: Country-specific deviations in AP
- $\beta_{1p[c]}$: Party-specific deviations in AP (within country)

**Controls:** Party size of rated party, ideological distance between respondent and rated party

**Substantive interpretation:**

- If $\beta_1 > 0$: Respondents rate their party anchor more warmly than other parties (affective polarization exists)
- If $\beta_3 > 0$: Explicit partisans show stronger affective polarization than implicit partisans (partisan identity amplifies ingroup favoritism)
- If $\beta_3 \approx 0$: Operational choice between explicit and implicit partisanship does not substantially affect AP estimates
- If $\sigma_{\text{AP,country}}^2$ is large: Attitudinal AP varies substantially across European democracies
- If $\sigma_{\text{AP,party}}^2$ is large: Some party families (e.g., radical parties) exhibit stronger affective polarization than others

#### Presentation Strategy

We report results in two stages to balance parsimony with comprehensive cross-national insight:

**Stage 1: Pooled European Estimates**

We first present population-average effects by extracting fixed effect posteriors and computing marginal predictions that average over the random effect distributions. Specifically, we report:

- **Fixed effects**: Posterior distributions for $\beta_1$ (average AP), $\beta_2$ (explicit partisan effect), and $\beta_3$ (AP × explicit interaction), presented as coefficient plots with 95% credible intervals
- **Predicted ratings by partisan type**: Marginal predictions for co-party vs. out-party ratings, separately for explicit and implicit partisans, computed by:
  - Drawing from the posterior: $\hat{Y}_{\text{explicit, coparty}} = \alpha_0 + \beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3$
  - Marginalizing over random effects: $\mathbb{E}[\hat{Y}] = \int \hat{Y} \cdot p(\alpha_c, \alpha_{p[c]}, \beta_{1c}) \, d\alpha_c \, d\alpha_{p[c]} \, d\beta_{1c}$
  - In practice, achieved by setting `re_formula = NULL` in **brms** prediction functions
- **Variance decomposition**: ICCs showing proportion of variance attributable to countries, parties, and respondents

This provides a clear, interpretable summary of AP patterns across the European sample.

**Stage 2: Country-Level Heterogeneity**

We then examine cross-national variation by extracting country-specific random effects and generating country-conditional predictions:

- **Country-varying AP effects**: Forest plot of $\beta_1 + \beta_{1c}$ for all 25 countries, showing which democracies exhibit strongest/weakest attitudinal polarization
- **Country-varying explicit/implicit gaps**: Plot of $\beta_3 + \beta_{3c}$ across countries, revealing where partisan operationalization matters most
- **Predicted country profiles**: For each country $c$, simulate predicted ratings:
  $$\hat{Y}_{c} = \alpha_0 + \alpha_c + \beta_1 + \beta_{1c} + \ldots$$
  Visualized as small-multiple plots showing co-party vs. out-party ratings by explicit/implicit status for each country
- **Country-level correlates (exploratory)**: Correlate country-specific AP estimates with institutional features (electoral system, polarization indices, party system fragmentation) to identify macro-level moderators

This two-stage approach allows readers to grasp the general European pattern before exploring the substantial cross-national diversity that the multilevel model captures.

### Study 2: Behavioral Consequences of Affective Polarization

**Research Question:** Do operational differences in partisanship alter the observed behavioral consequences of polarization?

**Outcome:** $Y_{ripc} = \text{Tokens}_{ripc}$ (token allocation to game partner, 0-100 scale)

**Model:**
$$
\text{Tokens}_{ripc} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{ripc}, \sigma^2)
$$

with $\mu_{ripc}$ specified as in the base model.

**Key parameters:**

- $\beta_1$: Behavioral AP effect (co-partisan favoritism in resource allocation)
- $\beta_3$: Differential behavioral AP between explicit and implicit partisans
- $\beta_{1c}$, $\beta_{1p[c]}$: Country- and party-varying behavioral AP

**Comparison with Study 1:** We evaluate whether $\beta_1^{\text{(Study 1)}} \neq \beta_1^{\text{(Study 2)}}$ and $\beta_3^{\text{(Study 1)}} \neq \beta_3^{\text{(Study 2)}}$ through posterior comparisons.

**Substantive interpretation:**

- If $\beta_1 > 0$: Respondents allocate more resources to co-partisans (behavioral discrimination exists)
- If $\beta_1^{\text{(Study 2)}} < \beta_1^{\text{(Study 1)}}$: Behavioral AP is weaker than attitudinal AP (attitudes do not fully translate to behavior)
- If $\beta_3 > 0$: Explicit partisans show stronger behavioral discrimination than implicit partisans
- If $\beta_3^{\text{(Study 2)}} \approx 0$ while $\beta_3^{\text{(Study 1)}} > 0$: Partisan identity matters for expressed attitudes but not for resource allocation decisions (key finding regarding attitude-behavior consistency)
- If $\sigma_{\text{AP,country}}^2$ is large: Behavioral consequences of partisanship vary substantially across institutional and cultural contexts

#### Presentation Strategy

We follow the same two-stage approach as Study 1, with an added cross-study comparison:

**Stage 1: Pooled European Estimates**

- **Fixed effects**: Posterior distributions for $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$, and $\beta_3$ from the behavioral model
- **Cross-study comparison**: Joint coefficient plot displaying $\beta_1^{\text{(thermo)}}$ vs. $\beta_1^{\text{(tokens)}}$ and $\beta_3^{\text{(thermo)}}$ vs. $\beta_3^{\text{(tokens)}}$, with posterior probability that attitudinal effects exceed behavioral effects:
  $$P(\beta_1^{\text{(thermo)}} > \beta_1^{\text{(tokens)}} \mid \text{data})$$
- **Predicted token allocations**: Average predicted tokens to co-partisan vs. out-partisan partners, by explicit/implicit status
- **Effect size comparison**: Calculate Cohen's $d$ or standardized mean differences for AP effects in both domains

**Stage 2: Country-Level Heterogeneity**

- **Country-specific behavioral AP**: Forest plot of $\beta_1 + \beta_{1c}$ across 25 countries
- **Attitude-behavior consistency by country**: Scatterplot with countries positioned by attitudinal AP (x-axis) vs. behavioral AP (y-axis), identifying countries where attitudes translate strongly/weakly to behavior
- **Country profiles**: Small-multiple plots showing predicted token allocations by co-partisan status and partisan type for each country
- **Correlation analysis**: Compute within-country correlation between attitudinal and behavioral AP estimates to assess cross-national variation in attitude-behavior coupling

This structure highlights the critical attitude-behavior gap while documenting its cross-national variability.

### Study 3: Partisan Sorting and Muslim Outgroup Salience

**Research Question:** How does partisan affective polarization interact with salient outgroup identities—specifically Muslimhood—to structure patterns of political sorting? Are there differences between explicit and implicit partisans?

We address this question in two complementary analyses:

#### Study 3a: Experimental Distribution (Uniform Muslim Assignment)

This analysis leverages the experimental design where Muslim identity was randomly assigned to game partners, creating a uniform (50%) distribution of Muslims across all partisan groups.

**Outcome:** $Y_{ripc} = \text{Tokens}_{ripc}$ (token allocation, 0-100 scale)

**Model:**
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{ripc} = &\alpha_0 + \alpha_c + \alpha_{p[c]} + \alpha_{i[pc]} \\
&+ \beta_1 \cdot \text{CoParty}_{r} \\
&+ \beta_2 \cdot \text{Explicit}_{i} \\
&+ \beta_3 \cdot (\text{CoParty}_{r} \times \text{Explicit}_{i}) \\
&+ \beta_4 \cdot \text{Muslim}_{r} \\
&+ \beta_5 \cdot (\text{CoParty}_{r} \times \text{Muslim}_{r}) \\
&+ \beta_6 \cdot (\text{Explicit}_{i} \times \text{Muslim}_{r}) \\
&+ \beta_7 \cdot (\text{CoParty}_{r} \times \text{Explicit}_{i} \times \text{Muslim}_{r}) \\
&+ \beta_{1c} \cdot \text{CoParty}_{r} + \beta_{1p[c]} \cdot \text{CoParty}_{r} \\
&+ \boldsymbol{X}_{ripc}'\boldsymbol{\beta}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{Muslim}_r$ indicates whether the game partner is identified as Muslim.

**Key parameters:**

- $\beta_4$: Main effect of partner being Muslim (Muslim penalty)
- $\beta_5$: Partisan sorting moderation by Muslim identity (does co-partisanship override Muslim outgroup status?)
- $\beta_6$: Differential Muslim penalty for explicit vs. implicit partisans
- $\beta_7$: Three-way interaction testing whether partisan sorting with Muslim partners differs by partisan type

**Substantive interpretation:**

- If $\beta_4 < 0$: Respondents allocate fewer resources to Muslim partners (religious outgroup discrimination)
- If $\beta_5 > 0$: Co-partisanship attenuates Muslim penalty (partisan identity overrides religious outgroup status)
- If $\beta_5 < 0$: Muslim identity overrides co-partisanship (religious outgroup status trumps partisan ingroup favoritism)
- If $\beta_6 < 0$: Explicit partisans show stronger anti-Muslim bias than implicit partisans
- If $\beta_7 > 0$: Explicit partisans are more willing than implicit partisans to override Muslim outgroup status when the partner is a co-partisan (stronger identity-based coalitional thinking)
- If $\beta_7 \neq 0$: The complexity of identity-based sorting differs between those with strong vs. weak partisan attachments

#### Study 3b: Empirical Distribution (Realistic Muslim-Partisan Sorting)

The experimental design assumes equal Muslim representation across parties. In reality, Muslim citizens are not uniformly distributed across the partisan landscape—they concentrate in certain parties (typically center-left, social democratic, or multicultural parties) and are nearly absent from others (especially radical right parties).

To assess how this real-world sorting conditions the interplay of partisan and religious identities, we conduct a **post-stratification analysis** that re-weights predictions according to the empirical distribution of Muslims across partisan groups.

**Estimation Strategy:**

1. **Estimate empirical Muslim-party distribution** from sample demographics:
   
   For each party anchor $p$ in country $c$, calculate:
   $$\hat{\pi}_{pc}^{\text{Muslim}} = \frac{\sum_{i \in p,c} \mathbb{I}(\text{Muslim}_i = 1)}{\sum_{i \in p,c} 1}$$
   
   This yields party-specific Muslim proportions (e.g., $\hat{\pi}_{\text{Greens}}^{\text{Muslim}} = 0.12$, $\hat{\pi}_{\text{AfD}}^{\text{Muslim}} = 0.01$).

2. **Generate predictions under empirical sorting**:
   
   Rather than marginalizing over the experimental 50-50 Muslim distribution, we compute weighted predictions:
   
   For each party $p$ and partisan type (explicit/implicit), predict:
   
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   \hat{Y}_{pc}^{\text{empirical}} = &\hat{\pi}_{pc}^{\text{Muslim}} \cdot \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \text{CoParty}=1, \text{Muslim}=1, p, c] \\
   &+ (1 - \hat{\pi}_{pc}^{\text{Muslim}}) \cdot \mathbb{E}[Y \mid \text{CoParty}=1, \text{Muslim}=0, p, c]
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   
   This represents expected tokens allocated to a co-partisan partner drawn from the realistic pool of party $p$ supporters.

3. **Compare across partisan contexts**:
   
   - For left-wing parties with higher Muslim representation, co-partisan interactions more frequently involve Muslim partners
   - For right-wing parties with minimal Muslim presence, co-partisan interactions rarely involve Muslim partners
   - This generates **asymmetric sorting patterns**: the "cost" of Muslim outgroup status on co-partisan favoritism varies systematically across the partisan spectrum

4. **Quantify sorting asymmetry**:
   
   Compute party-specific AP under empirical vs. experimental distributions:
   
   $$
   \Delta \text{AP}_p = \text{AP}_p^{\text{empirical}} - \text{AP}_p^{\text{experimental}}
   $$
   
   If $\beta_5 < 0$ (Muslim identity overrides co-partisanship), then left-wing parties with high Muslim representation should show *reduced* observed AP under realistic sorting compared to the experimental benchmark.

**Implementation:**
```r
# Step 1: Estimate Muslim proportions by party
muslim_props <- data %>%
  group_by(country, party_anchor) %>%
  summarise(
    prop_muslim = mean(respondent_muslim, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )

# Step 2: Generate predictions from Study 3a model
pred_grid <- expand_grid(
  country = unique(data$country),
  party_anchor = unique(data$party_anchor),
  coparty = 1,
  muslim = 0:1,
  explicit = 0:1
) %>%
  left_join(muslim_props)

predictions <- pred_grid %>%
  add_epred_draws(model_3a, re_formula = NULL)

# Step 3: Compute empirical-distribution weighted predictions
predictions_weighted <- predictions %>%
  group_by(country, party_anchor, explicit, .draw) %>%
  summarise(
    # Experimental (50-50)
    ap_experimental = .epred[muslim == 0] - mean(.epred[coparty == 0]),
    
    # Empirical (weighted by actual Muslim proportion)
    tokens_coparty_empirical = 
      prop_muslim * .epred[muslim == 1] + 
      (1 - prop_muslim) * .epred[muslim == 0],
    
    ap_empirical = tokens_coparty_empirical - mean(.epred[coparty == 0]),
    
    # Sorting bias
    sorting_bias = ap_empirical - ap_experimental
  )

# Step 4: Analyze asymmetry across partisan spectrum
predictions_weighted %>%
  group_by(party_anchor, explicit) %>%
  median_qi(sorting_bias) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(party_anchor, sorting_bias), 
             y = sorting_bias, 
             color = factor(explicit))) +
  geom_pointinterval() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Sorting Bias: How Realistic Muslim Distribution Affects AP",
       x = "Party Anchor",
       y = "Change in AP (Empirical - Experimental)",
       color = "Explicit Partisan")
```

**Substantive Interpretation:**

- **If sorting bias is negative for left-wing parties**: Higher Muslim representation among left-party supporters means co-partisan interactions more often cross religious lines, reducing observed behavioral AP when Muslim identity overrides partisanship
- **If sorting bias is near zero for right-wing parties**: Minimal Muslim representation means co-partisan interactions rarely involve religious outgroups, so observed AP matches experimental estimates
- **Cross-partisan asymmetry**: The interplay of partisan and religious sorting creates structural differences in how AP manifests across the ideological spectrum—a phenomenon masked by experimental uniform distribution

This extension reveals how **social identity complexity** (the intersection of partisan and religious identities) structures political behavior differently across partisan contexts, moving beyond experimental causal identification to assess real-world patterns of political sorting.

#### Presentation Strategy (Study 3)

**Stage 1: Pooled European Estimates (Study 3a - Experimental)**

- **Fixed effects**: Posterior distributions for $\beta_4$ (Muslim penalty), $\beta_5$ (co-party × Muslim), $\beta_6$ (explicit × Muslim), and $\beta_7$ (three-way interaction)
- **Predicted token allocations**: 2×2×2 design showing tokens by co-partisan status × Muslim identity × explicit partisan, averaged across Europe
- **Identity dominance test**: Calculate $P(\beta_5 > 0 \mid \text{data})$ to assess whether partisan identity overrides religious outgroup

**Stage 2: Country-Level Heterogeneity (Study 3a)**

- **Country-varying Muslim penalties**: Cross-national variation in $\beta_4$, reflecting differential salience of Muslim outgroup status
- **Country-varying identity interactions**: Variation in $\beta_5$ across countries, showing where partisan vs. religious identity dominates
- **Small-multiple plots**: Country-specific predictions for all eight conditions

**Stage 3: Partisan Sorting Under Realistic Distributions (Study 3b)**

- **Party-level Muslim representation**: Bar plot showing $\hat{\pi}_{pc}^{\text{Muslim}}$ across party families and countries
- **Sorting bias by party**: Forest plot of $\Delta \text{AP}_p$ showing which parties' observed AP is most affected by realistic Muslim distribution
- **Asymmetric polarization**: Comparison plot showing AP estimates under experimental vs. empirical distributions for left-wing, centrist, and right-wing parties
- **Structural inequality**: Discuss how differential Muslim sorting creates asymmetric exposure to cross-cutting identities across the partisan divide

This three-stage approach moves from experimental causal identification to realistic assessment of how partisan and religious sorting jointly structure European political behavior.

All models are estimated using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo via Stan (implemented through the **brms** package in R), with 4 chains of 4,000 iterations each (2,000 warmup), yielding 8,000 posterior draws for inference.

## Limitations

- Party-targeted attitudinal measures only

The attitudinal analysis relies exclusively on party-targeted thermometer ratings. It does not include direct citizen-targeted affect measures, limiting conclusions about horizontal affective polarization at the attitudinal level.

- Assumption underlying party-size weighting

Weighting by electoral party size—common in the literature—implicitly assumes that the probability of encountering partisans is proportional to vote share. This may not hold if certain parties (e.g., radical challenger parties) are socially more or less visible than their electoral strength suggests.

- Cross-sectional design (2019)

The data capture a specific pre-pandemic political context and allow inference only about the level (state) of affective polarization at that point in time. The design does not permit conclusions about temporal dynamics or trends.

- External validity of the experimental setting

Although the conjoint experiment approximates horizontal, citizen-level interactions, it remains an artificial setting. In real-world encounters, identities are rarely presented as explicit labels. Instead, they are inferred through cues and cognitive processes. This limits the direct generalizability of experimentally induced identity effects to everyday social interactions.

## Conclusion

(Preliminary thoughts)
In comparative multi-party systems:

- Affective polarization is not a single quantity.
- Its magnitude and cross-national configuration depend on:
      - measurement instrument (attitudinal/behavioral)
      - ingroup definition (implicit/explicit/all),
      - inclusion of non-partisans,
      - and whether polarization is conceptualized vertically or horizontally.

Rather than asking only *“How polarized are European democracies?”*,  
we ask:

How does conceptualization reshape what, and even who, we observe as polarized in multi-party contexts?

### Experimental setup {.appendix}

Before the behavioral games, @hahm2024divided presented respondents a short background information overview and instructions. For the dictator game, these were: *This game is played by pairs of individuals.* *Each pair is made up of a Player 1 and a Player 2.* *Each player will have some information about the other player, but you will not be told who the other players are during or after the experiment.* *The game is conducted as follows: A sum of 10 tokens will be provisionally allocated to Player 1 at the start of each round.* *Player 1 will then decide how much of the 10 tokens to offer to Player 2.* *Player 1 could give some, all, or none of the 10 tokens.* *Player 1 keeps all tokens not given to Player 2.* *Player 2 gets to keep all the tokens Player 1 offers.* *You will play this game three times with three different people.* In the trust game, the provided information and instruction were: *This game is played by pairs of individuals.* *Each pair is made up of a Player 1 and a Player 2.* *Each player will have some information about the other player, but you will not be told who the other players are during or after the experiment.* *Each player will receive 10 tokens.* *Player 1 then has the opportunity to give a portion of his or her 10 tokens to Player 2.* *Player 1 could give some, all, or none of the 10 tokens.* *Whatever amount Player 1 decides to give to Player 2 will be tripled before it is passed on to Player 2.* *Player 2 then has the option of returning any portion of this tripled amount to Player 1.* *Then, the game is over.* *Player 1 receives whatever he or she keeps from the original 10 tokens, plus anything returned to him or her by Player 2. Player 2 receives their original 10 tokens, plus whatever he or she keeps after returning any portion of the tripled amount to Player 1.* *You will play this game three times, with three different people.* *The more tokens you obtain, the more successful you will be.*

In both games respondents were shown a tabular overview of Player 2 after the instructions. @fig-example-profile shows an example of such a profile along with the interface respondents were provided to assign the 10 tokens. Each round, a new profile was displayed to respondents.

### Robustness {.appendix}
